english.html: led Sacrilegious. Thus Ovid, in some place, calls Lycurgus Sacrilegious, because he had despised the sacrifices of the god Bacchus. In the same way the Christians have generally called sacrilege every pollution and profanation of a sacred thing, every contempt and irreverence toward God, or toward the things instituted by him <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>: as for example, an abuse committed upon the sacrament of Baptism is rightly called Sacrilege <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>; so too a violence done to the Ministers of the Church <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. Likewise a piece of magic, inasmuch as the magician abuses holy words in the invocation of spirits <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. Thus he who traffics and makes merchandise of spiritual things is with good reason said to be Sacrilegious <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>; nay, he who disputes the power of the Prince, and calls into doubt whether the man whom he has chosen and called to his service is sufficient and worthy, deserves the title of Sacrilegious <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>. We read also that Sallust called Terentia, Cicero's wife, Sacrilegious <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>, because she was so troublesome, and so depraved in her manners, that Cicero, on his return from exile, was constrained to repudiate her <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>. Wherefore there is no doubt that those who despise, abuse and profane a thing so holy and sacred as marriage deserve to be called and judged Sacrilegious, and as such are worthy of death <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, the ordinary penalty of the sacrilegious, who have been at all times so odious that the ancients at times burned them alive <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>. And although pity and compassion for age, in other crimes and even in this one, ought to incline the judges to some gentleness and moderation of penalty <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>, nevertheless Aelian relates of a young child who of old had taken a gold plate from the crown of the goddess Diana: because, when afterwards there were set before him dolls and other little things (in which little children delight), he chose the plate again, he was condemned by the Athenians to death <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>.

notes.gloss: C. 9.9.29: sacrilegos autem nuptiarum gladio puniri oportet — the sacrilegious violators of marriage are to be punished with the sword; this is the text that makes adultery "sacrilege" and so carries Coras's whole annotation.

notes.citation: Digest 48.13 (Ad legem Iuliam peculatus), l. Sacrilegii (D. 48.13.7 = vulgate 48.13.6, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ſacrilegij. D. ad l. Iuli. pecul.
notes.gloss: The governor fixes the penalty of sacrilege according to the person, the thing, the time, age and sex: Ulpian knows of many condemned to the beasts, some burned alive (nonnullos etiam vivos exussisse), others hanged on the fork.

notes.citation: Digest 4.4 (De minoribus viginti quinque annis), l. Auxilium, § In delictis (D. 4.4.9.2, Ulpian); l. Sacrilegii, as at {l}
notes.original: l. auxilium. P. in dailect. D. de mino. l. ſacrilegij. alleg.
notes.gloss: In delictis autem minor annis viginti quinque non meretur in integrum restitutionem … nisi quatenus interdum miseratio aetatis ad mediocrem poenam iudicem produxerit — a minor has no restitution for his delicts, save that pity for his age may sometimes lead the judge to a moderate penalty. The print's dailect. is delict.

notes.original: Aelian au liure v de var. hiſtor. c. xvi
notes.gloss: The boy who took a gold leaf from the crown of Artemis; offered the leaf again among knucklebones and toys, he chose the leaf, and the Athenians put him to death as a sacrilegious person.

lines: les Sacrileges. Ainſi Ouide en, quelque lieu, nomme
Licurgus Sacrilege, partant qu'il auoit meſpriſé les ſa-
crifices du dieu Bachus. De meſmes les chreſtiens ont
generalement appelé ſacrilege, toute polution, & pro-
fanatiõ de choſe ſacree, meſpris, & irreuerẽce de Dieu,
ou des choſes par luy inſtituees {b}: comme par exemple,
vn abus commis au ſacrement de Bapteſme, eſt à bon
droit appelé Sacrilege {c}. vne violence auſſi faite aux Mi
niſtres de l'Egliſe {d}. Pareillement vne magie, d'autant
que le magicien abuſe des paroles ſainctes en inuoca-
tion d'eſprits {e}. Ainſi celuy qui traffique & fait marchã-
diſe des choſes ſpirituelles, à bõne raiſon eſt dit Sacri-
lege {f}. voire qui diſpute de la puiſſance du Prince, & re-
uoque en doute, ſi celuy eſt ſuffiſant, & digne, qui a eſté
par luy choiſi, & appelé à ſon ſeruice, merite le titre de
Sacrilege {g}, Nous liſons auſſi, que Saluſte appeloit Te-
rence, femme de Ciceron, Sacrilege {h}, par ce qu'elle e-
ſtoit faſcheuſe, & ſi deprauee en ſes meurs, qu'eſtant
Ciceron retourné d'exil, fut contraint la repudier {i}.
Dont ne faut doubter, que ceux qui meſpriſent, abu-
ſent, & profanent vne choſe ſi ſaincte & ſacree, qu'eſt le
mariage, ne meritent d'eſtre appellez, & iugez Sacrile-
ges: & comme tels, ne ſoyent dignes de mort {k}. peine
ordinaire des ſacrileges, leſquels ont eſté de tout tẽps
ſi odieux, que les anciens les õt toutesfois bruſlez tout
vifs {l}. Et bien que la pitié, & compaſſion de l'aage és
autres crimes, & meſmes en ceſtuy-ci, doyue incliner
les iuges à quelque douceur, & moderatiõ de peine {m}:
toutesfois Aelian recite d'vn ieune enfant, qui iadis
auoit prins vne tablete d'or de la couronne de la deeſ-
ſe Diane: par ce qu'en luy preſentant apres ces poupees
& autres petites choſes (auſquelles les petis enfans ſe
plaiſent il) choiſit de rechef la tablete, fut condamné
